summary:
Krea 2 is Krea.ai's diffusion transformer trained from scratch on thousands of GPUs in a single large InfiniBand-connected cluster, with no base checkpoint. It is released open source with two checkpoints: a raw pre-trained model for post-training and a fast turbo variant served in production on krea.ai. The model architecture is intentionally simple, porting ideas from LLM research into diffusion transformers.

At scale, training runs crash frequently and often silently (e.g., NCCL timeouts while dashboards stay green). The team's pragmatic response is to let jobs crash and restart on the same nodes; the same code and data often runs for 12-24 hours on subsequent attempts. Survivability comes from aggressive checkpointing to a paid, high-performance filesystem capable of ~1.8 TB/s reads, ~1 TB/s writes, and writing ~1 TB of checkpoints in under 30 seconds, allowing checkpoints every 20-30 minutes without delaying training. An earlier attempt with S3 as the checkpoint backend broke and eroded trust in stored data.

The talk emphasizes metrics over debugging individual nodes. Key signals include GPU temperature (any card above ~78°C is removed, not debugged), tensor-core utilization (which actually reflects useful work and rose as image resolution scaled from 128 to 1024 px, unlike the always-100% GPU utilization metric), and custom-collected InfiniBand counters covering throughput, wait times, packet errors, and NVLink errors, since most failures were cross-node communication and DCGM does not export these by default.

For scheduling, a queue layer adds two-tier gang scheduling and workload priority on top of Kubernetes, so training pods always preempt inference. A noted annoyance is that the queue's manually specified resource quotas drift as nodes phase in and out of maintenance, occasionally breaking gang scheduling; Kubernetes 1.15's built-in gang scheduling is mentioned as a possible alternative.

Production and training then share one cluster. When training needs GPUs, inference is migrated out to external providers and other clusters via a fake Kubernetes node built on virtual-kubelet: pods schedule onto the virtual node, a provider adapter translates them, and a reconciler keeps both sides in sync. Failure handling is delegated to Kubernetes via the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler — pods are simply marked failed and let Kubernetes recreate them. To avoid wasting GPUs when the cluster has spare capacity, the system applies Kubernetes taints: nodes with available GPUs are tainted so inference pods don't schedule there, and a descheduler, combined with a non-noExecute taint, gradually migrates pods back so production never goes down. Because diffusion transformer inference is small enough to run on almost any GPU, even degraded cards stay useful for inference, which keeps researchers unblocked.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Krea 2 is a diffusion transformer trained from scratch on thousands of GPUs and released open source with raw and turbo checkpoints.
Training at scale crashes constantly and often silently (NCCL timeouts with green dashboards); the pragmatic fix is to let jobs crash and re-run rather than debug each failure.
Aggressive checkpointing every 20-30 minutes to a paid, high-throughput filesystem (~1.8 TB/s reads, ~1 TB/s writes, ~1 TB checkpoint in under 30s) is what makes crash-heavy training survivable.
GPU utilization is described as 'a lie'; tensor-core utilization is the real signal and visibly climbs when training resolution scales from 128 to 1024 pixels.
Any GPU above ~78°C should be pulled and replaced, not debugged, because a warm card throttles and destabilizes the run.
InfiniBand counters (throughput, wait time, packet errors) and NVLink errors are not exported by DCGM and must be custom-collected; they caught most cross-node and some intra-node failures.
A queue with gang scheduling and priority tiers sits in front of Kubernetes, letting training preempt inference on a shared cluster.
A fake Kubernetes node built on virtual-kubelet migrates inference to external providers; pods are marked failed on errors and let Kubernetes recreate them via the HPA.
Kubernetes taints block inference pods from in-cluster GPUs and a descheduler gradually migrates pods back to in-cluster GPUs once training releases them, avoiding a production outage.
Diffusion transformer inference is small enough that even degraded GPUs (hot, failing, or low bus-width) can still serve it without complaints.

sections.title: Intro and what Krea 2 is
sections.summary: Gabriel introduces himself and Krea 2, a pre-trained-from-scratch diffusion transformer released open source with raw and turbo checkpoints serving on krea.ai. The model is intentionally simple, built for creative exploration, and was trained in-house on a large InfiniBand-connected cluster.

sections.title: Why crashes at scale are expected and often silent
sections.summary: As GPU count scales (128, 256, 512+), crash frequency rises and many failures are silent (e.g., NCCL timeouts with green dashboards). The team's learned response is not to debug each crash but to let it crash and re-run on the same nodes; identical code and data frequently run for 12-24 hours on the next attempt, and a Meta paper on expected failures was directionally right but Krea's runs were much shorter.

sections.title: Temperature-based hardware triage
sections.summary: GPU temperature is treated as a first-class signal: a single warmer card throttles and destabilizes training, so any GPU above ~78°C is removed and sent back to the provider instead of being debugged.

sections.title: GPU utilization vs tensor-core utilization
sections.summary: Standard GPU utilization reads 100% through pre-training but is described as a lie because it measures time busy, not useful work. Tensor-core utilization is used instead, and it visibly climbs as image resolution scales through 128, 256, 512, and 1024 pixels across pre-, mid-, and post-training.

sections.title: Custom InfiniBand and NVLink telemetry
sections.summary: Most of Krea's failures were cross-node communication, and DCGM does not export InfiniBand metrics or NVLink errors by default. The team built custom collection for InfiniBand throughput, wait time, packet counts, and errors, plus NVLink errors, which caught both inter-node fabric issues and some intra-node failures where individual machines looked otherwise healthy.

sections.title: Aggressive checkpointing against a fast filesystem
sections.summary: Constant crashes are made survivable by checkpointing aggressively to a paid, high-throughput filesystem (~1.8 TB/s reads, ~1 TB/s writes), producing ~1 TB checkpoints in under 30 seconds every 20-30 minutes without delaying training. An earlier attempt with S3 broke and caused loss of trust in stored data.

sections.title: Gang scheduling and training outranking production
sections.summary: A queue layer in front of Kubernetes provides gang scheduling and two-tier workload priority. Training pods always preempt inference, so researchers can launch jobs without thinking about GPUs and the cluster schedules them when capacity is available. A noted annoyance is that the queue's manually specified resource quotas drift as nodes phase in and out of maintenance, which can break gang scheduling; Kubernetes 1.15's built-in gang scheduling is mentioned as a possible alternative.

sections.title: Shared cluster and migrating inference out
sections.summary: One cluster serves both training and production, with training holding higher GPU priority than inference. To keep the public site up when training needs GPUs, inference is migrated out to external providers and other clusters through a fake Kubernetes node, with traffic flipped back gradually so the site never drops.

sections.title: How the fake node works: virtual-kubelet, providers, and HPA
sections.summary: The off-cluster migration is implemented on top of the open-source virtual-kubelet project. Kubernetes sees a fake node; pods scheduling onto it are handed to a provider adapter (e.g., a third-party cloud) via a reconciler. Failures are handled by simply marking pods failed and letting the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler recreate them, rather than trying to save the world on the off-cluster side.

sections.title: Taints and descheduler to stop wasting GPUs
sections.summary: To avoid wasting in-cluster GPUs on inference when training is idle, nodes with available GPUs are tainted so inference pods won't schedule there. When a training job claims all GPUs, the system removes the taint and inference schedules locally. When training finishes, the taint is reapplied and a descheduler (not a NoExecute taint, which would evict everything at once) gradually migrates pods back so production never drops. The system is driven by simple Prometheus metrics and is self-healing, though it needed calibration after early bugs.

sections.title: Inference runs on almost any GPU and hiring
sections.summary: Because diffusion transformer inference is small (unlike multi-node LLM inference), it runs even on degraded GPUs that are hot, falling off the bus, or otherwise misbehaving, which keeps researchers unblocked and the GPUs productive. Gabriel closes by noting Krea.ai is hiring, pointing to gabriel+hiring at krea.ai as the contact.
